title: The Story of Paper
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Before paper, people wrote on whatever they could find. The ancient Egyptians used papyrus, made by splitting the stems of a river reed into strips and pressing them together. In Europe, scribes used parchment, which was made from animal skin. Parchment lasted for centuries, but it was costly: a single large book might require the skins of a whole flock of sheep. For most of history, therefore, writing belonged to a small number of people who could afford it.

In China, early writers used strips of bamboo, which were heavy and awkward to store, or silk, which was light but very expensive. According to tradition, in the year 105 an official named Cai Lun presented the emperor with a new material made from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets. Archaeologists have since found fragments of paper that are older than his date, so he probably improved the method rather than invented it. Whoever deserves the credit, the new material was lighter than bamboo and far cheaper than silk, and its use spread quickly through the empire. His achievement was to make paper cheap enough for ordinary use.

The process was simple, which was one reason why it spread so widely. The raw materials were soaked in water for several days and then beaten into a soft pulp. The pulp was mixed with water in a large vat. A worker dipped a screen made of fine bamboo strips into the vat and lifted it out, leaving a thin layer of fibres on the screen as the water drained away. The wet sheets were stacked and pressed to squeeze out the remaining water, and finally they were hung up to dry.

For several centuries the Chinese guarded the secret of papermaking. It moved west along the Silk Road, the network of trade routes that linked China with the Mediterranean, and by the eighth century paper was being made in Samarkand and Baghdad. A popular story claims that Chinese prisoners taught the craft after a battle in 751, but historians doubt this, since merchants had been carrying paper along the same routes for years and local workers could have learned from them.

In the Islamic world, paper had an enormous effect. Mills in Baghdad produced it in large quantities, and cheap paper encouraged the growth of libraries, bookshops and schools. Scholars copied and translated works of mathematics, medicine and astronomy, and many of these texts later reached Europe. Europeans were slower to accept the new material. Some officials distrusted it as flimsy and refused to accept important documents written on paper, and the first European mills did not appear until the twelfth century, in Spain. Once people saw how cheap and convenient the material was, however, resistance faded, and by the end of the Middle Ages paper was in everyday use in most of Europe.

The arrival of the printing press in the middle of the fifteenth century changed the situation completely. Printers needed large amounts of paper, and demand soon outran the supply of rags, which were still the main raw material. By the nineteenth century the shortage was so serious that manufacturers were searching for alternatives. The solution, discovered in the 1840s, was to make pulp from wood. It was far cheaper than rag, and it made possible the mass-produced newspapers and cheap books that had once been unimaginable.

Predictions that computers would create a paperless world have not come true, and the world uses more paper today than it did fifty years ago. Environmental groups have criticised the industry for cutting down forests, and manufacturers have responded by planting new trees and by recycling. In many countries more than half of the paper produced now comes from used paper, so the fibres that Cai Lun's workers beat into pulp nearly two thousand years ago are still being reused.
